claim: Beta-HPVs, including type 8 (HPV8), are associated with nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC) in immunocompromised individuals including people with a rare genetic disorder epidermodysplasia verruciformis and organ transplant recipients.
source: Beta-HPVs, including type 8 (HPV8), are associated with nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC) in immunocompromised individuals including people with a rare genetic disorder epidermodysplasia verruciformis and organ transplant recipients (Bouwes Bavinck et al., 2018; Bouwes Bavinck et al., 2001; Dell'Oste et al., 2009; Sichero et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Beta-HPV infections are hypothesized to promote cancer formation by making UV-induced DNA damage more mutagenic.
source: Because beta-HPV infections are not persistent in immunocompetent people, they are hypothesized to promote cancer formation by making UV-induced DNA damage more mutagenic (Hufbauer et al., 2015; Spriggs and Laimins, 2017; Wendel and Wallace, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The E6 protein from HPV8 (8E6) impairs DNA repair.
source: In support of this hypothesis, our group and others have used in vitro and in vivo systems to demonstrate that the E6 protein from HPV8 (8E6) impairs DNA repair (Hufbauer et al., 2015; Rollison et al., 2019; Wallace et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research including authors' own work

claim: The interaction with and destabilization of p300 is a key mechanism by which 8E6 hinders DNA repair.
source: The interaction with and destabilization of p300 is a key mechanism by which 8E6 hinders DNA repair (Dacus and Wallace, 2021; Howie et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: P300 is an acetyltransferase that regulates transcription by chromatin remodeling.
source: P300 is an acetyltransferase that regulates transcription by chromatin remodeling (Ait-Si-Ali et al., 2000; Dutto et al., 2018; Goodman and Smolik, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: By binding p300, 8E6 decreases the abundance of multiple DNA repair proteins including ATR, ATM, BRCA1, and BRCA2.
source: By binding p300, 8E6 decreases the abundance of multiple DNA repair proteins including ATR, ATM, BRCA1, and BRCA2 (Wallace et al., 2015; Wallace et al., 2013; Wallace et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: 8E6 lowers the activation of ATM and ATR signaling, decreasing the cellular response to UV-damaged DNA.
source: This lowers the activation of ATM and ATR signaling, decreasing the cellular response to UV-damaged DNA (Snow et al., 2019; Wallace et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The limited ability to repair UV damage increases the frequency with which UV causes replication forks to collapse into double strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA.
source: The limited ability to repair UV damage increases the frequency with which UV causes replication forks to collapse into double strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA (Pathania et al., 2011; Rapp and Greulich, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Homologous recombination (HR) is minimally mutagenic, but restricted to in S/G2 phase when the sister chromatids can serve as homologous templates.
source: Homologous recombination (HR) is minimally mutagenic, but restricted to in S/G2 phase when the sister chromatids can serve as homologous templates (Orthwein et al., 2015; Shibata et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: When HR is inhibited, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is used to repair DSBs.
source: When HR is inhibited (by cell cycle position, mutation to repair factors, or artificially), non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is used to repair DSBs (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: NHEJ can occur throughout the cell cycle, as it does not require a homologous template.
source: NHEJ can occur throughout the cell cycle, as it does not require a homologous template.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about NHEJ mechanism

claim: NHEJ is more mutagenic than HR because NHEJ generates and ligates blunt ends to fix a DSB.
source: However, because NHEJ generates and ligates blunt ends to fix a DSB, it is more mutagenic than HR (Mao et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: 8E6 attenuates both HR and NHEJ by degrading p300.
source: We have shown that 8E6 attenuates both HR and NHEJ by degrading p300 (Hu et al., 2020; Hu and Wallace, 2022c; Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to authors' own published research

claim: 8E6 does not block the initiation of NHEJ or HR.
source: Notably, 8E6 does not block the initiation of NHEJ or HR.
evidence: Statement based on authors' previous findings

claim: NHEJ initiation occurs when DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit (DNA-PKcs) complexes at DSBs and activates itself by autophosphorylation (pDNA-PKcs).
source: NHEJ initiation occurs when DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit (DNA-PKcs) complexes at DSBs and activates itself by autophosphorylation (pDNA-PKcs) (Davis et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: DNA-PKcs autophosphorylation occurs readily in the presence of 8E6.
source: This occurs readily in the presence of 8E6.
evidence: Statement based on authors' observations

claim: 8E6 prevents the resolution of pDNA-PKcs repair complexes and attenuates other downstream steps in NHEJ.
source: However, 8E6 prevents the resolution of pDNA-PKcs repair complexes and attenuates other downstream steps in NHEJ (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' published research

claim: 8E6 allows the HR pathway to initiate, before hindering the resolution of RAD51 repair complexes.
source: Similarly, 8E6 allows the HR pathway to initiate, before hindering the resolution of RAD51 repair complexes (Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' published research

claim: Cells respond to 8E6-associated inhibition of NHEJ by trying to complete HR during G1.
source: We recently demonstrated that cells respond to 8E6-associated inhibition of NHEJ by trying to complete HR during G1 (Hu et al., 2022a; Hu et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citations to authors' recent published research

claim: 8E6 leads to persistent unresolved RAD51 repair complexes formed during G1.
source: This ultimately leads to persistent unresolved RAD51 repair complexes formed during G1.
evidence: Statement based on authors' previous findings

claim: When NHEJ and HR fail, alternative end joining (Alt-EJ) is tasked with completing DSB repair.
source: When NHEJ and HR fail, another mutagenic repair pathway known as alternative end joining (Alt-EJ) is tasked with completing DSB repair (Iliakis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: 8E6 promotes DSB repair by Alt-EJ.
source: Here, we use reporter constructs and small molecule inhibitors of DNA repair factors to demonstrate that 8E6 promotes DSB repair by Alt-EJ
evidence: Demonstrated using reporter constructs and inhibitors in this study

claim: The use of Alt-EJ is the indirect result of initiating NHEJ when the pathway cannot be completed.
source: Here, we use reporter constructs and small molecule inhibitors of DNA repair factors to demonstrate that 8E6 promotes DSB repair by Alt-EJ and to show that the use of Alt-EJ is the indirect result of initiating NHEJ when the pathway cannot be completed.
evidence: Demonstrated using reporter constructs and inhibitors in this study

claim: 8E6 increases terminal Alt-EJ in HFK cells.
source: Transient transfection of this reporter into HFK LXSN and HFK 8E6 demonstrated that 8E6 increased terminal and imbedded Alt-EJ (Figure 1B–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1

claim: 8E6 increases imbedded Alt-EJ in HFK cells.
source: Transient transfection of this reporter into HFK LXSN and HFK 8E6 demonstrated that 8E6 increased terminal and imbedded Alt-EJ (Figure 1B–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1

claim: PARP-1 inhibition blocks Alt-EJ.
source: We confirmed that PARP-1 inhibition blocked Alt-EJ using the reporter system described above (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Confirmed using reporter system and olaparib treatment, shown in Figure 2

claim: PARP-1 inhibition does not significantly alter DSB repair in HFK LXSN cells.
source: PARP-1 inhibition did not significantly alter DSB repair in HFK LXSN cells (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by pH2AX analysis after zeocin treatment, shown in Figure 2

claim: PARP-1 inhibition significantly delayed DSB repair in HFK 8E6 cells.
source: In contrast, PARP-1 inhibition significantly delayed DSB repair in HFK 8E6 cells (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by pH2AX analysis after zeocin treatment, shown in Figure 2

claim: Most DSB repair occurs via either HR or NHEJ, with Alt-EJ serving as a fail-safe machinery should these pathways fail.
source: This is consistent with the established view that most DSB repair occurs via either HR or NHEJ, with Alt-EJ serving as a fail-safe machinery should these pathways fail (Iliakis et al., 2015; Patterson-Fortin and D'Andrea, 2020; Simsek and Jasin, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: 8E6 does not increase the abundance of polymerase theta (POLθ).
source: This analysis did not find any notable changes in POLθ abundance (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: There are no significant differences in viability between HFK LXSN and HFK 8E6 cells when grown in media containing a gradient (0–50 μM) of ART558 concentrations.
source: There were no significant differences in viability between HFK LXSN and HFK 8E6 cells when grown in media containing a gradient (0–50 μM) of ART558 concentrations (Figure 3C)
evidence: Demonstrated by MTT assay shown in Figure 3

claim: ART558 delayed DSB repair in HFK 8E6 cells but not in HFK LXSN cells.
source: ART558 delayed DSB repair in HFK 8E6 cells but not in HFK LXSN cells, indicating that 8E6 promoted repair by TMEJ (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by pH2AX analysis after zeocin treatment, shown in Figure 3

claim: 8E6 promotes repair by TMEJ (polymerase theta mediated end joining).
source: ART558 delayed DSB repair in HFK 8E6 cells but not in HFK LXSN cells, indicating that 8E6 promoted repair by TMEJ (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Inferred from differential effect of POLθ inhibitor on HFK 8E6 vs LXSN cells

claim: 8E6 inhibits multiple types of DNA-PKcs-independent end joining, including but not limited to TMEJ.
source: We interpret these data as evidence that 8E6 inhibits multiple types of DNA-PKcs-independent end joining, including but not limited to TMEJ.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of the magnitude of effects from PARP1 vs POLθ inhibition

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition increases both imbedded and terminal Alt-EJ in HFK LXSN cells.
source: As expected, DNA-PKcs inhibition increased both imbedded and terminal Alt-EJ in HFK LXSN cells (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Alt-EJ reporter assay with NU7441 treatment, shown in Figure 4

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition results in a further significant increased use of Alt-EJ in HFK 8E6 cells.
source: DNA-PKcs inhibition resulted in a further significant increased use of Alt-EJ in HFK 8E6 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by Alt-EJ reporter assay with NU7441 treatment

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition makes DSB repair more efficient in HFK 8E6 cells.
source: Supporting our hypothesis, DNA-PKcs inhibition made DSB repair more efficient (less pH2AX) in HFK 8E6 cells (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pH2AX analysis after zeocin treatment with NU7441, shown in Figure 5

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition increases the persistence of RAD51 in HFK LXSN cells.
source: As we have previously reported (Hu et al., 2022a), DNA-PKcs inhibition increased the persistence of RAD51 in HFK LXSN (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by RAD51 foci analysis with NU7441 treatment, shown in Figure 5

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition increases the rate of RAD51 resolution in HFK 8E6 cells.
source: However, DNA-PKcs inhibition increased the rate of RAD51 resolution in HFK 8E6 (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by RAD51 foci analysis with NU7441 treatment, shown in Figure 5

claim: Ligase IV inhibition delayed DSB repair in both HFK LXSN and HFK 8E6 cells.
source: Ligase IV inhibition delayed DSB repair in both HFK LXSN and HFK 8E6 cells (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by pH2AX analysis after zeocin treatment with SCR7, shown in Figure 5

claim: Restoration of DSB repair in HFK 8E6 specifically requires inhibition of an early NHEJ step, rather than inhibition of a later step in the pathway.
source: Thus, restoration of DSB repair in HFK 8E6 specifically requires inhibition of an early NHEJ step, rather than inhibition of a later step in the pathway.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of DNA-PKcs inhibition vs ligase IV inhibition

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition increases the frequency of HFK LXSN in G1 that contained RAD51 foci.
source: DNA-PKcs inhibition increased the frequency of HFK LXSN in G1 that contained RAD51 foci (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RAD51 and cyclin E co-staining with NU7441 treatment, shown in Figure 6

claim: Without DNA-PKcs inhibition, 8E6 increased the frequency of cells in G1 that had RAD51 foci.
source: Without DNA-PKcs inhibition, 8E6 increased the frequency of cells in G1 that had RAD51 foci.
evidence: Demonstrated by RAD51 and cyclin E co-staining analysis

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition prevented 8E6 from promoting the formation of RAD51 repair complexes during G1.
source: However, DNA-PKcs inhibition prevented 8E6 from promoting the formation of RAD51 repair complexes during G1.
evidence: Demonstrated by RAD51 and cyclin E co-staining with NU7441 treatment

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition increases HR efficiency in vector control U2OS cells (U2OS LXSN).
source: In vector control U2OS cells (U2OS LXSN), NU7441 increases HR efficiency (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by DR-GFP reporter assay with NU7441 treatment, shown in Figure 7

claim: NHEJ and HR compete for access to DSBs.
source: This is consistent with the established idea that NHEJ and HR compete for access to DSBs (Bunting et al., 2010; Chapman et al., 2012; Orthwein et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: 8E6 in U2OS cells (U2OS 8E6) decreased HR efficiency.
source: As previously reported, 8E6 in U2OS cells (U2OS 8E6) decreased HR efficiency (Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' published research

claim: DNA-PKcs inhibition did not prevent 8E6 from hindering HR.
source: However, DNA-PKcs inhibition did not prevent 8E6 from hindering HR (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by DR-GFP reporter assay with NU7441 treatment, shown in Figure 7

claim: U2OS cells expressing 8E6 with the residues responsible for binding p300 deleted (U2OS 8E6Δ132–136) were similar to vector control in HR efficiency.
source: Consistent with a p300-dependent mechanism (see next section for more details), U2OS cells expressing 8E6 with the residues responsible for binding p300 deleted (U2OS 8E6Δ132–136) were similar to vector control (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by DR-GFP reporter assay, shown in Figure 7

claim: 8E6Δ132–136 shows similar Alt-EJ frequency with U2OS LXSN.
source: Consistent with the p300-dependent mechanism, 8E6Δ132–136 shows similar Alt-EJ frequency with U2OS LXSN (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Alt-EJ reporter assay, referenced as Figure 7A-B but likely Figure 8A-B based on context

claim: P300 knockout led to increases in both terminal and imbedded Alt-EJ.
source: P300 knockout led to increases in both terminal and imbedded Alt-EJ (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Alt-EJ reporter assay in p300 knockout cells, shown in Figure 8

claim: P300 inhibitor CCS1477 increased both terminal and imbedded Alt-EJ.
source: Consistently, CCS1477 increased both terminal and imbedded Alt-EJ (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Alt-EJ reporter assay with CCS1477 treatment, shown in Figure 8

claim: HFK without p300 displayed an increased frequency of RAD51 staining in G1 that could be overcome by DNA-PKcs inhibition.
source: Further confirming a p300-dependent mechanism of action, HFK without p300 displayed an increased frequency of RAD51 staining in G1 that could be overcome by DNA-PKcs inhibition (Figure 9C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by RAD51 and cyclin E co-staining in p300 knockout cells with NU7441 treatment, shown in Figure 9

claim: Inhibition of p300 alone increased the frequency of RAD51 staining in G1.
source: Inhibition of p300 alone increased the frequency of RAD51 staining in G1 as did DNA-PKcs inhibition alone (Figure 9E–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by RAD51 and cyclin E co-staining with CCS1477 treatment, shown in Figure 9

claim: RAD51 staining in G1 was not increased by dual application of p300 and DNA-PKcs inhibition.
source: However, RAD51 staining in G1 was not increased by their dual application.
evidence: Demonstrated by RAD51 and cyclin E co-staining with combined CCS1477 and NU7441 treatment

claim: Whole genome sequencing yielded 933,163,972 high-quality paired-end sequence reads for LXSN and 624,472,714 reads for 8E6.
source: This yielded 933,163,972 high-quality paired-end sequence reads for LXSN and 624,472,714 reads for 8E6 (Table 1).
evidence: Reported sequencing data shown in Table 1

claim: Normalizing LXSN reads to the same number as 8E6 and alignment to the human genome yielded 92.4% genome coverage for both.
source: Normalizing LXSN reads to the same number as 8E6 and alignment to the human genome yielded 92.4% genome coverage for both and slightly more read depth for LXSN (mean 45.4 for LXSN compared to 44.6 for 8E6) (Table 2).
evidence: Reported sequencing analysis data shown in Table 2

claim: Variant calling showed one variation every 3 kb in LXSN compared to one every 3333 bases in 8E6.
source: Variant calling including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and insertions or deletions (indels) were also more for LXSN cells than 8E6 expressing cells with one variation every 3 kb in LXSN compared to one every 3333 bases in 8E6 (Table 3).
evidence: Reported variant analysis data shown in Table 3

claim: There is a significantly higher frequency of accumulated short deletions (2–29 bp) in the 8E6 cell line (86.75% in 8E6 compared to 82.33% in LXSN, p-value = 2.2e-16).
source: Despite a larger number of annotated indels unique to LXSN (168,005 for LXSN compared to 104,322 for 8E6), this revealed a significantly higher frequency of accumulated short deletions (2–29 bp) in the 8E6 cell line (86.75% in 8E6 compared to 82.33% in LXSN, p-value = 2.2e-16).
evidence: Reported statistical analysis of deletion frequencies from whole genome sequencing

claim: The frequency of short Alt-EJ type deletions was most significant for deletions with short (≤10 bp) stretches of flanking microhomology.
source: The frequency of short Alt-EJ type deletions was most significant for deletions with short (≤10 bp) stretches of flanking microhomology (Table 4).
evidence: Reported analysis of deletion characteristics shown in Table 4

claim: 8E6 increases the frequency of short deletions with very short stretches of flanking microhomology.
source: We show that 8E6 increases the frequency of short deletions with very short stretches of flanking microhomology.
evidence: Demonstrated by whole genome sequencing analysis

claim: The ability to promote Alt-EJ seems to have evolved in two separate genes in the HPV family (once in HPV16 E7 and once in HPV8 E6).
source: Thus, the ability to promote Alt-EJ seems to have evolved in two separate genes in the HPV family (once in HPV16 E7 and once in HPV8 E6) (Leeman et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from comparison with published research on HPV16 E7

claim: HPV16 E7 increases the use of Alt-EJ.
source: Induction of Alt-EJ is not limited to HPV8 as a recent report demonstrated that a different HPV protein from a different genus of HPV (HPV16 E7) also increases the use of Alt-EJ (Leeman et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: HPV positive head and neck squamous cell carcinomas have an elevated frequency of mutations with signatures of repair by Alt-EJ.
source: Further, HPV positive head and neck squamous cell carcinomas and other cancers with downregulated TGF-b signaling have an elevated frequency of mutations with signatures of repair by Alt-EJ (Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Cancers with downregulated TGF-b signaling have an elevated frequency of mutations with signatures of repair by Alt-EJ.
source: Further, HPV positive head and neck squamous cell carcinomas and other cancers with downregulated TGF-b signaling have an elevated frequency of mutations with signatures of repair by Alt-EJ (Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: By promoting DSB repair by Alt-EJ, 8E6 increases the risk of mutations associated with DSBs while allowing cells to avoid the apoptosis that would be associated with an unrepaired DSB.
source: By promoting DSB repair by Alt-EJ, 8E6 increases the risk of mutations associated with DSBs while allowing cells to avoid the apoptosis that would be associated with an unrepaired DSB.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of the biological significance of their findings

claim: This study supports the hypothesis that beta-HPV promotes cancer formation by increasing genomic instability.
source: Broadly, this study supports the hypothesis that beta-HPV promotes cancer formation by increasing genomic instability.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of how their findings support the broader hypothesis

claim: 8E6 promotes Alt-EJ by binding p300, an acetyltransferase that facilitates DSB repair by HR and NHEJ.
source: Further, using small molecule inhibitors, CRISPR/CAS9 gene knockout, and HPV8 E6 mutant, we find that HPV8 E6 promotes Alt-EJ by binding p300, an acetyltransferase that facilitates DSB repair by HR and NHEJ.
evidence: Demonstrated using multiple experimental approaches including inhibitors, knockout, and mutant

claim: At least some of the Alt-EJ repair promoted by 8E6 occurs through polymerase theta dependent end joining.
source: At least some of this repair occurs through a subset of Alt-EJ known as polymerase theta dependent end joining.
evidence: Demonstrated using POLθ inhibitor experiments

claim: 8E6 caused an increased frequency of deletions bearing the microhomology signatures of Alt-EJ.
source: Finally, whole genome sequencing analysis showed HPV8 E6 caused an increased frequency of deletions bearing the microhomology signatures of Alt-EJ.
evidence: Demonstrated by whole genome sequencing analysis

claim: In HFK 8E6 cells, DSBs become three- to fourfold more persistent when PARP1 is inhibited.
source: This analysis demonstrated that in HFK 8E6 cells, DSBs become three- to fourfold more persistent when PARP1 is inhibited but only ~1.5-fold more persistent when POLθ is inhibited.
evidence: Inferred from quantitative analysis of pH2AX persistence with inhibitors

claim: In HFK 8E6 cells, DSBs become only ~1.5-fold more persistent when POLθ is inhibited.
source: This analysis demonstrated that in HFK 8E6 cells, DSBs become three- to fourfold more persistent when PARP1 is inhibited but only ~1.5-fold more persistent when POLθ is inhibited.
evidence: Inferred from quantitative analysis of pH2AX persistence with inhibitors

claim: 8E6 promotes DSB repair that is dependent on PARP1 and to a lesser extent on POLθ.
source: Thus, 8E6 promotes DSB repair that is dependent on PARP1 and to a lesser extent on POLθ.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of PARP1 vs POLθ inhibition

claim: NHEJ initiation blocks DSB repair by other pathways, including Alt-EJ.
source: NHEJ initiation blocks DSB repair by other pathways, including Alt-EJ (Patterson-Fortin and D'Andrea, 2020; Simsek and Jasin, 2010; Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Alt-EJ is primarily used when there are defects in either HR or NHEJ.
source: This is compatible with the idea that Alt-EJ is primarily used when there are defects in either HR or NHEJ (Deriano and Roth, 2013; Simsek and Jasin, 2010; Truong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: P300 restricts DSB repair by Alt-EJ.
source: We also show that p300 restricts DSB repair by Alt-EJ
evidence: Demonstrated by p300 knockout and inhibitor experiments

claim: At least some of the DSB repair defects caused by p300 loss or 8E6 expression can be overcome by inhibition of DNA-PKcs.
source: We also show that p300 restricts DSB repair by Alt-EJ and that at least some of the DSB repair defects caused by p300 loss or 8E6 expression can be overcome by inhibition of DNA-PKcs.
evidence: Demonstrated by DNA-PKcs inhibitor experiments in p300 knockout and 8E6 expressing cells

claim: 8E6 impairs apoptosis by degrading BAK.
source: However, 8E6 impairs apoptosis by degrading BAK, which complicates the interpretation of these data.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about 8E6 function

claim: U2OS may contain mutations (such as an ATR mutation) that change the mechanisms of DSB repair pathway choice.
source: We also acknowledge that U2OS may contain mutations (such as an ATR mutation) that change the mechanisms of DSB repair pathway choice (Elbakry et al., 2021; Juhász et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The known ways that 8E6 alters DSB repair are consistent in U2OS and primary (HFK) cells.
source: However, the known ways that 8E6 alters DSB repair are consistent in U2OS and primary (HFK) cells, suggesting that results obtained in U2OS cells can be extrapolated to other cell types (Hu et al., 2020; Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to authors' published research

claim: Transient β-HPV infections may promote tumorigenesis by causing mutations.
source: Similarly, by showing that 8E6 promotes Alt-EJ, a mutagenic DSB repair pathway, we provide evidence in support of the idea that transient β-HPV infections may promote tumorigenesis by causing mutations (Tommasino, 2019; Viarisio et al., 2018; Wendel and Wallace, 2017).
evidence: Authors' interpretation supported by citations to published research

claim: Unrepaired DSBs are highly lethal.
source: Unrepaired DSBs are highly lethal, thus we infer a strong selective pressure for HPV (a non-lytic virus) to find alternative way(s) to repair DSBs.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about DSB lethality

claim: There is a strong selective pressure for HPV (a non-lytic virus) to find alternative way(s) to repair DSBs.
source: Unrepaired DSBs are highly lethal, thus we infer a strong selective pressure for HPV (a non-lytic virus) to find alternative way(s) to repair DSBs.
evidence: Authors' inference based on the lethality of unrepaired DSBs and HPV biology

claim: Beta-HPVs are ubiquitous and transiently infect cutaneous epithelia in the general population.
source: Beta genus human papillomaviruses (beta-HPVs) are ubiquitous and transiently infect cutaneous epithelia in the general population (Bouwes Bavinck et al., 2018; Gheit, 2019; Neale et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The contribution of beta-HPV infections to NMSC in the general population is unclear.
source: However, the contribution of beta-HPV infections to NMSC in the general population is unclear.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap in the field

claim: Beta-HPV infections are not persistent in immunocompetent people.
source: Because beta-HPV infections are not persistent in immunocompetent people, they are hypothesized to promote cancer formation by making UV-induced DNA damage more mutagenic
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about beta-HPV infection characteristics

claim: Cells have multiple DSB repair mechanisms.
source: Cells have multiple DSB repair mechanisms.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about DNA repair

claim: Whenever possible cells use HR to fix DSBs as it allows them to avoid mutations.
source: Whenever possible cells use HR to fix DSBs as it allows them to avoid mutations.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about DNA repair pathway preference

claim: The persistent RAD51 repair complexes that form in HFK 8E6 cells occur during G1.
source: The persistent RAD51 repair complexes that form in HFK 8E6 cells occur during G1 (Hu et al., 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' published research

claim: 8E6 retains its ability to alter DNA repair in U2OS cells.
source: U2OS cells are routinely used to probe 8E6 biology because 8E6 retains its ability to alter DNA repair in these cells (Hu et al., 2020; Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to authors' published research

claim: Loss of PARP-1 activity only reduces polymerase theta mediated end joining (TMEJ) by two- to fourfold.
source: Specifically, loss of PARP-1 activity only reduces polymerase theta mediated end joining (TMEJ) by two- to fourfold (Luedeman et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Alt-EJ is an umbrella term that includes any end joining event that does not require DNA-PKcs activity.
source: Alt-EJ is an umbrella term that includes any end joining event that does not require DNA-PKcs activity.
evidence: Definition of Alt-EJ based on established knowledge

claim: While most Alt-EJ relies on PARP-1, a subset of Alt-EJ can occur when PARP-1 activity is impaired.
source: While most Alt-EJ relies on PARP-1, a subset of Alt-EJ can occur when PARP-1 activity is impaired.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Alt-EJ mechanisms

claim: Repair by Alt-EJ can frequently result in indels with characteristic sequence signatures of flanking microhomology.
source: Repair by Alt-EJ can frequently result in indels with characteristic sequence signatures of flanking microhomology.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Alt-EJ repair signatures

claim: The Alt-EJ deletions promoted by 8E6 appear more frequently as short deletions (2–29 bp) bearing short stretches of microhomology (2–10 bp).
source: These Alt-EJ deletions appear more frequently as short deletions (2–29 bp) bearing short stretches of microhomology (2–10 bp) (Table 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole genome sequencing analysis shown in Table 4

claim: The increase in HFK LXSN cells treated with DNA-PKcs inhibitor did not reach the levels of Alt-EJ in mock-treated HFK 8E6 cells.
source: However, the increase in HFK LXSN cells did not reach the levels of Alt-EJ in mock-treated HFK 8E6 cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Alt-EJ frequencies across conditions

claim: DSBs were more persistent in mock-treated 8E6 cells than LXSN cells.
